title: Stoic in love
hook: love people knowing they're mortal, and love them more

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Meditations, where Marcus says skip the disgust and simply return. Your line was return.

Late at night, a parent stands in the doorway of a child's room. The child is asleep, one arm flung over the side of the bed. And out of nowhere, a thought arrives that parents rarely say out loud: what if something happened to them? It comes with a stab of fear, and right behind it, a wave of love so strong it almost hurts. Epictetus had something to say about that exact doorway, and it is hard to hear.
screen: `A PARENT IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHAT IF SOMETHING HAPPENED?` → `FEAR, THEN A WAVE OF LOVE.`

segments.voice: First, the hard line. In the Handbook, section three, Epictetus says: if you kiss your child or your spouse, remind yourself that you're kissing a human being. Then, if they die, you won't be overwhelmed. In the Discourses he goes further: when you kiss your child, whisper to yourself, tomorrow you may die. A student objects that it's an ill-omened thing to say. Epictetus answers: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested? It's just naming something natural. Second, the honest reaction. Some readers find this cold. Epictetus's stated aim is to protect the mind from being wrecked by loss, and some hear it as holding back love to avoid pain. That reading is fair to his words, and not every reader, or every Stoic since, accepts it. Third, another way it can land. Marcus Aurelius copied this teaching into his own notebook, the harvest reply and all. For some readers today, remembering that the people they love are mortal doesn't make the love smaller. It makes it sharper, more awake: no more assuming there'll be endless Tuesdays. Seneca, in a letter on grief, urges enjoying friends eagerly while you have them, because no one knows how long that will be. Fourth, put together, the porch can leave you with this: they are mortal, and they are loved. Not one instead of the other. The first is the reason to say the second out loud.
screen: `YOU'RE KISSING A HUMAN BEING.` · `SOME READERS FIND IT COLD.` · `MORTALITY MAKES LOVE MORE AWAKE.` · `SAY IT WHILE YOU CAN.` · then, large: `MORTAL, AND LOVED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you love, their face, their laugh, the way they walk into a room, and gently remember that they're mortal, as you are. Notice what comes, fear, tenderness, maybe both, without pushing either away. Then let the love come forward, and find one thing you haven't said to them lately.
Handbook, Epictetus's short teaching text, where he says: when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a mortal human being. Today's word.
Your line: mortal, and loved. Knowing the first never has to shrink the second. Day six hundred eighty-four, done.

howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners briefly remember the mortality of those they love, and use it as a reason to express their love now; others find Epictetus's version too cold and set it aside.

chat.says: Why would a Stoic remind himself, kissing his child, that the child is mortal?
options: To meet loss without being wrecked; some readers find it makes love more awake.
Because Stoics believed thinking about it would keep the harm away.
To prepare to forget them quickly if the worst should happen.
chat.meaning: Epictetus says it protects the mind from being overwhelmed by loss. Some readers find remembering mortality makes love sharper, so they say it out loud.
